body: Nineteen minutes on hold, and the same eight bars have come round often enough that the woman listening has started to hear the join. She is sitting at a kitchen table at twenty to three on a Thursday afternoon with a ring binder open in front of her. The binder holds letters in date order, each one with a reference number she now knows by heart. She is holding a pen she is not using. Her son’s school shoes are on the radiator, stuffed with newspaper, because the drain at the back is still not right. When the line finally picks up she has to spell the surname twice and then explain, from the beginning again, what happened in April of last year.
Nobody films that. There is no version of that Thursday afternoon anybody would put in front of a congregation, and it is the fourteenth month of it.
The testimony has a fixed shape. There was a bad time, God moved, and here I am. It is told from the far side and it is compressed, and the compression is where all the damage gets done.

It is worth taking the word storm literally, because everyone already understands this about weather and forgets it about lives. The storm is the short part. A gale runs for a night. What comes after it runs for months: the tarpaulin, the assessor who cannot come until the twelfth, the tree still lying across the lane, the smell that will not leave the hall carpet, the letter explaining which part of the damage the policy does not cover, the neighbours who are magnificent for a week and then quite reasonably go back to their own lives. Everybody photographs the storm. Nobody photographs month five of the clearing up, and month five is where the actual work is.

This band is programmed for the second part. The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air, running through the night as well as the day, and the hours nobody would schedule an event in are exactly the hours they are built to cover.

That is expensive in a way that never shows. Hours that run at three in the morning to a handful of people cost the same as any others, and there is no way to make them look impressive afterwards. They are carried anyway, because the people awake then are not the people an event was designed for. Every testimony you have heard was edited to end at the good bit, and everybody listening quietly concluded that theirs was going wrong. The hours after midnight exist for the ones doing that arithmetic.

The selection is not dishonest, which is what makes it hard to argue with. Church media runs on stories, and a story needs an ending; an unresolved account cannot be told because nobody can say what it is an account of yet. So what gets platformed is what has finished, which is a small and unrepresentative sample of what is going on in the room. Nobody decided to teach that the Christian life is a series of resolutions with short gaps between them. It got taught anyway, by accident, as a by-product of what is tellable.

The dial resists that shape, mostly by being a dial. A station is not an event. It has no start, no finish and no outcome to report; it holds one frequency permanently, no two stations share a number, and the schedule is published before it airs rather than assembled around whoever happens to be listening. It cannot congratulate you at the end because there is no end. What it can do is still be there on the Thursday, which is a much smaller promise and a far more useful one.
None of this is an argument against telling what God has done. It is an argument about what the telling leaves out.

Because the testimony night is a good institution and the stories in it are true. Rescues happen. People do come out of things they had no business coming out of, and saying so out loud is right, and biblical. What the format cannot do is keep company. It is an account of an event, delivered by somebody standing on dry land, to a room in which a good proportion of people are still in the water. Four minutes for the bad time and the rest for the rescue tells the person in month fourteen that the ratio in their own life is wrong, and they will believe it, because they have no other figures to compare it against.
The rescue is the short part. Nearly all of it is the clearing up.

A man of fifty-five wakes at ten past three, which is when he wakes most nights now, about a year after the business went. He does not lie there, because he has learnt that lying there is worse. He goes down in his socks so as not to wake his wife, fills a glass at the tap and puts the radio on low, and stands at the sink looking at the garden, which needs doing and will not get done this month either. He does not pray, exactly. He works through the same three items in the same order and gets no further with them than he did on Tuesday. At about four he goes back up. Nothing has been settled. He is at work by seven and nobody there knows he was awake.

That is the mechanism, and it is unglamorous on purpose. Nothing in that hour resolved anything. It got a man from ten past three to four o’clock in a room that had a sound in it, which is the whole of what was available that night.

The honest thing to say is that some of this never becomes a story. Some clearing up simply goes on and then stops going on, and there is no moment anybody could point to. The debts get paid and the marriage still ends. The trust never fully comes back with two of the four people whose trust it was, and they are entitled to that. Nobody is owed a rescue on a schedule, and pretending otherwise is how the compressed testimony does its damage.

But the absence of an ending is not a defect in the account. It is the condition most of Scripture is actually written from — the long middle, where the sea has been crossed and the land is not in sight and there is nothing to do but keep walking and eat what turns up. That stretch is precisely why something has to run without an audience. A gathering needs people to gather. A station does not, and the hour at three in the morning is not a lesser hour for having almost nobody in it.

So the case is straightforward. The part of your life that is hardest to talk about is the part you are most likely to be in, and it is the part almost nothing is made for. Programming for the clearing up means assuming the storm has passed and that this has not made the week easy, which is the true position of a great many people sitting quietly in church on a Sunday.
All of which is theory until about three in the morning. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns, country and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards, 40 frequencies carrying 29 languages between them. It all runs to a schedule published before it airs, and it runs at the hours when nothing else is running.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 305.40 — Torah Sings. It is the Angel Songs flagship, voiced by Zev Inspire, and it carries the largest catalogue on this dial; the family calls it the workhorse station, which is the right word for it. The testimony everybody quotes ends at the sea. What follows the sea in the actual text is forty years of walking, bread that had to be gathered every single morning, and a law given to people who were no longer in danger and not yet home — which is the clearing up, written down, at length, by people who did not edit it to end at the good bit. Sunrise Praise runs at six and Evening Worship at eight, every day, whether or not the day deserved it.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually own. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for at ten past three in the morning, which is how the next station gets built and how the ones already on air get better.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not evaluate it; you have a ring binder and a phone queue and quite enough to be assessing. Put HM 305.40 on the next time you are up at an hour you did not choose, and let it run while you stand at the sink. It will not resolve anything and it is not going to give you an ending. It will simply be there again tomorrow, in the same place, at the same number, which is the only thing that has ever been much use in the fourteenth month.
